(x,t,t_0)$ is defined as
\begin{equation}\label{eq:154}
	\mathcal{I}^{\rm L}(x,t,t_0)
	:=
	\left\{ 
	\mathbf{U}= \left( \rho, y, z \right)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^3 
	: 
	
	\begin{array}{r}
		v \in [v^{\rm L}_{\min}(x,t,t_0), v^{\rm L}_{\max}(x,t,t_0)] \\  
		w \in [w^{\rm L}_{\min}(x,t,t_0), w^{\rm L}_{\max}(x,t,t_0)] \\
		c \in [c^{\rm L}_{\min}(x,t,t_0), c^{\rm L}_{\max}(x,t,t_0)] 
	\end{array}
	\right\},
\end{equation}
where the local bounds of Riemann invariants are defined as
\begin{align*}
	v^{\rm L}_{\min}(x,t,t_0) &:= \min_{\xi \in \mathcal{X}} v(\xi,t_0),
	& w^{\rm L}_{\min}(x,t,t_0) &:= \min_{\xi \in  \mathcal{X}} w(\xi,t_0),
	& c^{\rm L}_{\min}(x,t,t_0) &:= \min_{\xi \in \mathcal{X}} c(\xi,t_0), 
	\\
	v^{\rm L}_{\max}(x,t,t_0) &:= \max_{\xi \in  \mathcal{X}} v(\xi,t_0),
	& w^{\rm L}_{\max}(x,t,t_0) &:= \max_{\xi \in  \mathcal{X}} w(\xi,t_0),
	& c^{\rm L}_{\max}(x,t,t_0) &:= \max_{\xi \in \mathcal{X}} c(\xi,t_0).

\label{rmk:435}
	Although the constraint $v \le v_{\max}$ is not directly addressed, the considered constraint $w \le w_{\max}$ actually implies another upper bound for $v$:
	\[
	v = w-p(\rho,z) \le w_{\max} - p(\rho,z)
	\le
	\begin{dcases}
		w_{\max} 
		& 
		{\rm if }~ \gamma > 0,
		\\
		w_{\max} - v_{\rm ref} \log (\min_x \rho)
		& {\rm if }~ \gamma = 0.
	\end{dcases}
	\]
	As one will see in the numerical experiments, this upper bound on $v$ can also help mitigate overshoots in $v$ in the numerical results.

In the following, we will prove that U_theta in Omega_1. First, the positivity of rho_theta can be obtained by rho_theta = (1 - theta) rho_0 + theta rho_1 ge min\rho_1,rho_0\ > 0. Since w_theta = fracy_thetarho_theta = frac (1 - theta) y_0 + theta y_1 (1 - theta) rho_0 + theta rho_1 & = left( frac(1 - theta) rho_0(1 - theta) rho_0 + theta rho_1 right) w_0 + left( frac theta rho_1 (1 - theta) rho_0 + theta rho_1 right) w_1, \\ c_theta = fracz_thetarho_theta = frac (1 - theta) z_0 + theta z_1 (1 - theta) rho_0 + theta rho_1 & = left( frac(1 - theta) rho_0(1 - theta) rho_0 + theta rho_1 right) c_0 + left( frac theta rho_1 (1 - theta) rho_0 + theta rho_1 right) c_1, namely, w_theta (resp. c_theta) is a convex combination of w_0 and w_1 (resp. c_0 and c_1), we have w_theta in [w_min,w_max] (resp. c_theta in [c_min,c_max]). Thus, U_theta in Omega_1 and Omega_1 is convex. \\ sf Part III: Now, let us assume U_0 and U_1 in Omega_2. The positivity of z_theta can be obtained by z_theta = (1 - theta) z_0 + theta z_1 ge min\z_1,z_0\ > 0. Additionally, we need to show v_theta ge v_min. Consider a function of rho and z defined as eta(rho,z) := rho (v_min + p(rho, z)) = y+rho(v_min-v) , such that for state U = (rho,y,z)^top, the condition v(U) ge v_min is equivalent to y ge eta(rho,z). Since y_theta ge eta(rho_theta,z_theta) for theta = 0 and 1, in order to prove v_theta ge v_min, or equivalently, y_theta ge eta(rho_theta,z_theta), we only need to show that the function eta(rho,z) is convex for (rho,z) in R_+ times R_+. To this end, we will show that its Hessian matrix H is positive semi-definite. In the case of gamma = 0, the Hessian matrix is given by \( H = diag\ v_ref/rho, 0 \, \) which is clearly positive semi-definite. In the case of gamma > 0, \[ H = fracv_refgammaz^kapparho^gamma-kappa-1 left(cc (kappa-gamma)(kappa-gamma-1) z^2 & -kappa(kappa-gamma-1)zrho \\ -kappa(kappa-gamma-1)zrho & kappa (kappa-1) rho^2 right), \] and the determinants of its principle minors are given by H_11 = fracv_refgammaz^kappa+2rho^gamma-kappa-1 (kappa-gamma)(kappa-gamma-1) ge 0, H_22 = fracv_refgammaz^kapparho^gamma-kappa+1 kappa (kappa-1) ge 0, \\ |H| = fracv_refgammaz^kappa+2rho^gamma-kappa-1 left[ (gamma-kappa)(gamma-kappa+1) kappa(kappa-1)-kappa^2(gamma-kappa+1)^2 right] ge 0. Thus, we conclude that U_theta in Omega_2 and Omega_2 is convex. \\ sf Part IV: Since both Omega_1 and Omega_2 are convex, their intersection Omega is also convex.
nodes.raw_latex:
{\sf Part I}: 
	The set $\Omega_0$ is clearly convex.
	
	\noindent{\sf Part II}: 
	For any two states $\mathbf{U}_0 = (\rho_0,y_0,z_0)^\top$ and $\mathbf{U}_1 = (\rho_1,y_1,z_1)^\top \in \Omega_1$, and any $\theta \in [0,1]$, let us denote $ (\rho_\theta, y_\theta, z_\theta)^\top = (1 - \theta) \mathbf{U}_0 + \theta \mathbf{U}_1$. In the following, we will prove that $\mathbf{U}_\theta \in \Omega_1$. 
	First, the positivity of $\rho_\theta$ can be obtained by
	$\rho_\theta = (1 - \theta) \rho_0 + \theta \rho_1 \ge \min\{\rho_1,\rho_0\} > 0$.
	Since
	\begin{align*}
		w_\theta
		=
		\frac{y_\theta}{\rho_\theta}
		=
		\frac
		{(1 - \theta) y_0 + \theta y_1}
		{(1 - \theta) \rho_0 + \theta \rho_1}
		&
		=
		\left(
		\frac{(1 - \theta) \rho_0}{(1 - \theta) \rho_0 + \theta \rho_1}
		\right)
		w_0
		+
		\left(
		\frac
		{\theta \rho_1}
		{(1 - \theta) \rho_0 + \theta \rho_1}
		\right)
		w_1,
		\\
		c_\theta
		=
		\frac{z_\theta}{\rho_\theta}
		=
		\frac
		{(1 - \theta) z_0 + \theta z_1}
		{(1 - \theta) \rho_0 + \theta \rho_1}
		& 
		=
		\left(
		\frac{(1 - \theta) \rho_0}{(1 - \theta) \rho_0 + \theta \rho_1}
		\right)
		c_0
		+
		\left(
		\frac
		{\theta \rho_1}
		{(1 - \theta) \rho_0 + \theta \rho_1}
		\right)
		c_1,
	\end{align*}
	namely, $w_\theta$ (resp. $c_\theta$) is a convex combination of $w_0$ and $w_1$ (resp. $c_0$ and $c_1$), we have $w_\theta \in [w_{\min},w_{\max}]$ (resp. $c_\theta \in [c_{\min},c_{\max}]$). Thus, $\mathbf{U}_\theta \in \Omega_1$ and $\Omega_1$ is convex. \\
	
	{\sf Part III}: Now, let us assume $\mathbf{U}_0$ and $\mathbf{U}_1 \in \Omega_2$. The positivity of $z_\theta$ can be obtained by 
	$z_\theta = (1 - \theta) z_0 + \theta z_1 \ge \min\{z_1,z_0\} > 0$.
	Additionally, we need to show $v_\theta \ge v_{\min}$.
	Consider a function of $\rho$ and $z$ defined as
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:406}
		\eta(\rho,z)
		:=
		\rho (v_{\min} + p(\rho, z))
		=
		y+\rho(v_{\min}-v)
		,
	\end{equation}
	such that for state $\mathbf{U} = (\rho,y,z)^\top$, the condition $v(\mathbf{U}) \ge v_{\min}$ is equivalent to $y \ge \eta(\rho,z)$. Since $y_\theta \ge \eta(\rho_\theta,z_\theta)$ for $\theta = 0$ and $1$, in order to prove $v_\theta \ge v_{\min}$, or equivalently, $y_\theta \ge \eta(\rho_\theta,z_\theta)$, we only need to show that the function $\eta(\rho,z)$ is convex for $(\rho,z) \in \mathbb{R}_+ \times \mathbb{R}_+$. To this end, we will show that its Hessian matrix $\mathbf{H}$ is positive semi-definite.
	In the case of $\gamma = 0$, the Hessian matrix is given by
	\(
	\mathbf{H}
	= {\rm diag}\{ v_{\rm ref}/\rho, 0  \}, 
	\)
	which is clearly positive semi-definite.
	In the case of $\gamma > 0$,
	\[
	\mathbf{H}
	=
	\frac{v_{\rm ref}}{\gamma}z^{\kappa}\rho^{\gamma-\kappa-1}
	\left(\begin{array}{cc} 
		(\kappa-\gamma)(\kappa-\gamma-1) z^2
		& -\kappa(\kappa-\gamma-1)z\rho \\ 
		-\kappa(\kappa-\gamma-1)z\rho
		& \kappa (\kappa-1) \rho^2
	\end{array}\right),
	\]
	and the determinants of its principle minors are given by
	\begin{gather*}
		\mathbf{H}_{11}
		= 
		\frac{v_{\rm ref}}{\gamma}z^{\kappa+2}\rho^{\gamma-\kappa-1}
		(\kappa-\gamma)(\kappa-\gamma-1)
		\ge 0,
		\quad
		\mathbf{H}_{22}
		= 
		\frac{v_{\rm ref}}{\gamma}z^{\kappa}\rho^{\gamma-\kappa+1}
		\kappa (\kappa-1) 
		\ge 0,
		\\
		|\mathbf{H}|
		=

	We first consider the case of $\gamma > 0$. In this case,
	\[
	h_{z_*}(\rho_*, z_*;\rho,z)
	= 
	\frac{\kappa v_{\rm ref}}{\gamma} z_*^{\kappa-2} \rho_*^{\gamma-\kappa}

	\gamma \rho_*z_*
	+
	(\kappa-\gamma-1) \rho z_*
	-
	(\kappa-1) \rho_* z
	\Big],
	\]
	which, due to $\kappa \ge \gamma+1$ and the positivities of $\rho_*$, $z_*$, $\rho$, and $z$, implies that
	\[
	\begin{dcases}
		h_{z_*}(\rho_*, z_*;\rho,z) \ge 0
		&
		{\rm if} ~  z_* \ge \frac{(\kappa-1) \rho_* z}{\gamma \rho_* + (\kappa-\gamma-1) \rho} =: z_\star,
		\\
		h_{z_*}(\rho_*, z_*;\rho,z) < 0
		&
		{\rm otherwise}.
	\end{dcases}
	\]
	Therefore,
	\begin{align*}
		h(\rho_*, z_*;\rho,z)
		\ge 
		h\left(\rho_*, z_\star;\rho,z\right)
		= \rho p (\rho, z) - \frac{v_{\rm ref}}{\gamma} z \, \rho_*^{\gamma - \kappa + 1} z_\star^{\kappa - 1}
		=:	\tilde{h}(\rho_*;\rho,z).
	\end{align*}
	Taking partial derivative of $\tilde{h}(\rho_*;\rho,z)$ with respect to $\rho_*$ gives
	\[
	\tilde h_{\rho_*}(\rho_*;\rho,z)
	=
	v_{\rm ref} \frac{\kappa - \gamma - 1}{\kappa - 1} 
	(\rho_* -\rho) \, \rho_* ^{\gamma -\kappa -1} z_\star^\kappa,
	\]
	which implies $\tilde h(\rho_*;\rho,z)$ is increasing with respect to $\rho_*$ if $\rho_* \ge \rho$, and decreasing if $\rho_* < \rho$.
	Therefore, $\tilde h(\rho_*;\rho,z)	\ge \tilde h(\rho;\rho,z)$, and we finally have
	\[
	h(\rho_*,z_*;\rho,z) 
	\ge \tilde h(\rho_*;\rho,z)
	\ge \tilde h(\rho;\rho,z)
	=
	h(\rho,z;\rho,z) = 0.
	\]

	\[

	=

	\rho \log \rho - \rho \log \rho_* + \rho_* - \rho
	\right)
	=: \hat{h}(\rho_*;\rho).
	\]

	\]

			\ge 0
			,
		\end{aligned}

	=
	y - \rho \big( v_{\min} + p(\rho,z)\big)
	=
	\rho \big( v(\mathbf{U}) - v_{\min}\big)
	\ge 0.
	\]
	Therefore, it holds that $\mathbf{U} \in \Omega_2$. The proof is completed.

			2\mathrlap{ \raisebox{0.6 pt}{$\widecheck{\phantom{\mathbf{U}}}$} } \mathrlap{ \raisebox{-0.6 pt}{$\widehat{\phantom{\mathbf{U}}}$} } \mathbf{U} \cdot \mathbf{n}_* + 2s_*
			& =

			~\right] 
			\cdot \mathbf{n}_* + 2 s_*
			\\
			& =  
			\widehat{\mathbf{U}} \cdot \mathbf{n}_* + \widecheck{\mathbf{U}} \cdot \mathbf{n}_*
			+
			\alpha^{-1}
			\left(
			\widehat{\mathbf{F}} \cdot \mathbf{n}_*
			-

			+
			v_{\min} s_*
			-
			v_{\min} s_*
			\right)
			+
			2 s_*
			\\
			& =  
			\widehat{\mathbf{U}} \cdot \mathbf{n}_* + \widecheck{\mathbf{U}} \cdot \mathbf{n}_*	+ 2s_*
			-
			\alpha^{-1} \left( \widecheck{\mathbf{F}} \cdot \mathbf{n}_* + v_{\min} s_* \right)
			-

			(\widecheck{\mathbf{U}} \cdot \mathbf{n}_* + s_*)
			\\
			&
			\hspace{5mm} +
			\left(\widehat{\mathbf{U}} \cdot \mathbf{n}_*+s_*\right)
			-
			\alpha^{-1}
			\left( \left|v(\widehat{\mathbf{U}})\right|+\frac{s_*}{\hat{\rho}}\right)
			(\widehat{\mathbf{U}} \cdot \mathbf{n}_* + s_*)
			\\
			& =

			\left(\alpha-\left|v(\widehat{\mathbf{U}})\right|-\frac{s_*}{\hat{\rho}}\right)
			+

			\left(\widecheck{\mathbf{U}} \cdot \mathbf{n}_*+s_*\right)
			\left(\alpha-\left|v(\widecheck{\mathbf{U}})\right|-\frac{s_*}{\check{\rho}}\right).
		\end{aligned}
	\end{equation}

	.

nodes.statement: We adopt the OE procedure instead of the traditional TVB limiter to control numerical oscillations. The main reason for this choice is that while the TVB limiter requires the solution to be decomposed into its characteristics for an effective simulation, the OE procedure does not necessitate such a decomposition. For more information on OEDG methods, readers are referred to .

\begin{equation}\label{BPOE}
	\begin{aligned}
		&\widetilde{\mathbf{U}}_h^{n, 1}  = \mathbf{U}^{n}_h + \Delta t_n \mathcal{L} \left(\mathbf{U}^{n}_h \right), 
		& 
		 \widehat{\mathbf{U}}_h^{n, 1} & = \mathcal{F}_\tau \widetilde{\mathbf{U}}_h^{n, 1}, 
		&
		 \mathbf{U}_j^{n, 1} & = \mathcal{B} \left( \widehat{\mathbf{U}}_j^{n, 1}; {\Omega}_j^{n,1} \right) \; \forall j,
		\\
		& \widetilde{\mathbf{U}}_h^{n, 2} = \frac{3}{4} \mathbf{U}_h^{n} + \frac{1}{4} \left( \mathbf{U}_h^{n, 1} + \Delta t_n \mathcal{L} (\mathbf{U}_h^{n, 1} ) \right), 
		& 
		\widehat{\mathbf{U}}_h^{n, 2} & = \mathcal{F}_\tau \widetilde{\mathbf{U}}_h^{n, 2}, 
		&
		\mathbf{U}_j^{n, 2} & = \mathcal{B} \left( \widehat{\mathbf{U}}_j^{n, 2}; {\Omega}_j^{n,2} \right) \; \forall j,
		\\
		&\widetilde{\mathbf{U}}_h^{n,3} = \frac{1}{3} \mathbf{U}_h^{n} + \frac{2}{3} \left( \mathbf{U}_h^{n, 2} + \Delta t_n \mathcal{L} (\mathbf{U}_h^{n, 2} ) \right), 
		& 
		\widehat{\mathbf{U}}_h^{n,3} & = \mathcal{F}_\tau \widetilde{\mathbf{U}}_h^{n,3},
		&
		\mathbf{U}_j^{n,3} & = \mathcal{B} \left( \widehat{\mathbf{U}}_j^{n,3}; {\Omega}_j^{n,3} \right) \; \forall j,
		\\
		&\mathbf{U}^{n+1}_h = \mathbf{U}^{n,3}_h.
	\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

\label{lem:1467}
	For any $d \in \mathbb{N}^+$, consider a convex set $\mathcal{R} \in \mathbb{R}^d$, a continuous and concave function $H(\mathbf{U}): \mathcal{R} \mapsto \mathbb{R}$, and a threshold $\varepsilon \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $\mathcal{R}_\varepsilon := \{\mathbf{U} \in \mathcal{R} : H(\mathbf{U}) \ge \varepsilon \}$ is not empty.
	For any $\overline{\mathbf{U}} \in \mathcal{R}_\varepsilon$ and $\widehat{\mathbf{U}} \in \mathcal{R}$, let us define
	\[
	\Theta(\overline{\mathbf{U}},\widehat{\mathbf{U}},H,\varepsilon) :=
	\begin{dcases}
		1 & \textrm{if }H(\widehat{\mathbf{U}}) \ge \varepsilon, \\
		\textrm{ the unique solution of } H\big(\mathcal{U}(\theta;\overline{\mathbf{U}},\widehat{\mathbf{U}})\big) = \varepsilon \textrm{ in } [0,1] & \textrm{if }H(\widehat{\mathbf{U}}) < \varepsilon.
	\end{dcases}
	\]
	where $\mathcal{U}(\theta;\overline{\mathbf{U}},\widehat{\mathbf{U}}) := \theta \widehat{\mathbf{U}} + (1-\theta) \overline{\mathbf{U}}$.
	It holds that
	(i) the set $\mathcal{R}_\varepsilon$ is convex; 
	(ii) the equation $H\big(\mathcal{U}(\theta;\overline{\mathbf{U}},\widehat{\mathbf{U}})\big) = \varepsilon$ has a unique solution in $[0,1]$ for $\widehat{\mathbf{U}} \not \in \mathcal{R}_\varepsilon$; and
	(iii) for any $\theta \in \big[0,\Theta(\overline{\mathbf{U}},\widehat{\mathbf{U}},H,\varepsilon)\big]$, $\mathcal{U}(\theta;\overline{\mathbf{U}},\widehat{\mathbf{U}}) \in \mathcal{R}_\varepsilon$, that is, $H(\mathcal{U}(\theta;\overline{\mathbf{U}},\widehat{\mathbf{U}})) \ge \varepsilon$.

Since $\mathbf{U}_j(x) \in \mathbb{P}^k$, the $L$-point Gauss--Lobatto quadrature holds exactly:
	\[
	\overline{\mathbf{U}}_j
	= \frac{1}{\Delta x} \int_{I_j} \mathbf{U}_j(x) \, \textrm{d}x
	= \sum_{\ell = 1}^L \omega^{\tt GL}_\ell \mathbf{U}_j(x^{\tt GL}_{j,\ell}).
	\]
	Since $\omega^{\tt GL}_1 = \omega^{\tt GL}_L$, $x^{\tt GL}_{j,1} = x_{j-\frac12}$, $x^{\tt GL}_{j,L} = x_{j+\frac12}$, we can rewrite \eqref{eq:2121} as
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:2265}
		\overline{\mathbf{U}}^*_j
		=
		\sum_{\ell = 2}^L 
		\omega^{\tt GL}_\ell \mathbf{U}_j(x^{\tt GL}_{j,\ell})
		+
		(\omega^{\tt GL}_1-\lambda)
		\mathbf{U}_j(x^{\tt GL}_{j,1})
		+
		(\omega^{\tt GL}_1-\lambda)
		\mathbf{U}_j(x^{\tt GL}_{j,L})
		+
		\lambda \mathbf{U}_j^{-}
		+
		\lambda \mathbf{U}_j^{+},
	\end{equation}
	where $\lambda := \alpha \frac{\Delta t}{\Delta x} \le \omega^{\tt GL}_1$, and
	$\mathbf{U}_j^{\pm} := \mathcal{S}_{\tt GLF}(\mathbf{U}^{\pm}_{j-\frac12},\mathbf{U}^{\pm}_{j+\frac12})$.
	\Cref{thm:1471} implies that $\mathbf{U}^{\pm}_j \in \Omega$.

	$
	\overline{\mathbf{U}}_j^n 
	= 
	\frac{1}{\Delta x} \int_{I_j} \mathbf{U}^n_j(x) \, \textrm{d} x
	=
	\sum_{\ell = 1}^{L} \omega^{\tt GL} \mathbf{U}^n_j(x^{\tt GL}_{j,\ell}),
	$
	which decomposes $\overline{\mathbf{U}}_j^n$ as a convex combination of $\mathbf{U}^n_j(x^{\tt GL}_{j,\ell}) \in \Omega^n$, which leads to $\overline{\mathbf{U}}_j^n \in \Omega^{n} = \Omega^{n,0} \subseteq \Omega^{n,1}$ due to the convexity of $\Omega$ (\Cref{lem:466}) and the hierarchy of global invariant domains (\Cref{lem:1889}).
	Additionally, all the cell-edge values of $\mathbf{U}^n_h$ belong to $\Omega^{n,1}$, since
	(i) For $j = 1,\dots,N_x$, $\mathbf{U}^n_h(x_{j-\frac12}^{+}) = \mathbf{U}^n_j(x^{\tt GL}_{j,1}) \in \Omega^{n} = \Omega^{n,0} \subseteq \Omega^{n,1}$, $\mathbf{U}^n_h(x_{j+\frac12}^{-}) = \mathbf{U}^n_j(x^{\tt GL}_{j,L}) \in \Omega^{n} = \Omega^{n,0} \subseteq \Omega^{n,1}$;
	(ii) By \Cref{lem:1872}, $\mathbf{U}^n_h(x_{\frac12}^{-}) \in \Omega^{n,1}$ and $\mathbf{U}^n_h(x_{N_x+\frac12}^{+}) \in \Omega^{n,1}$.
	Therefore, we can apply \Cref{lem:2154} on $\mathbf{U}^n_h$ to obtain $\mathrlap{ \raisebox{1.2 pt}{$\overline{\phantom{\mathbf{U}}}$} } \mathrlap{ \raisebox{-0.9 pt}{$\widetilde{\phantom{\mathbf{U}}}$} } \mathbf{U}^{n,1}_j \in \Omega^{n,1}$ for all $j$,
	and then \Cref{lem:1625b} to obtain $\mathrlap{ \raisebox{1.2 pt}{$\overline{\phantom{\mathbf{U}}}$} } \mathrlap{ \raisebox{-0.9 pt}{$\widehat{\phantom{\mathbf{U}}}$} } \mathbf{U}^{n,1}_j \in \Omega^{n,1}$ for all $j$.

	$\mathbf{U}^{n,s}_h(x^{\tt GL}_{j,\ell}) \in \Omega^{n,s}$ for any $j$, $\ell$, and $s = 2,3$.

The computational domain is \([0,1]\) with periodic boundary conditions at both boundaries. The exact solution reads rho(x, t) = 0.05 Big[ 1 + cos(pi (x - 0.15 \, t)) Big] + 10^-8, v(x, t) equiv 0.15, c(x,t) equiv 1. We compute the numerical solution up to \( t = 0.05 \) using the BP-OEDG scheme. The \( L_1 \) errors of the obtained numerical results are presented in Table , confirming the expected third-order accuracy. Please note that near-vacuum states appear in the solution. Employing nonBP-OEDG schemes for this example may produce numerical solutions with negative density, which can lead to simulation failure. The \( L_1 \) errors of the obtained numerical results are presented in Table , confirming the expected third-order accuracy. Please note that near-vacuum states appear in the solution. Employing nonBP-OEDG schemes for this example may produce numerical solutions with negative density, which can lead to simulation failure. For example, if the nonBP-OEDG method is used, the simulation would fail due to negative density in the numerical results; see Creftab:2830 for the failure time. nodes.statement: This example verifies the effectiveness and necessity of the OE procedure for eliminating oscillations. Consider the Riemann problem with initial data: \[ (rho,v,c)(x,0) = (0.8,0.1,1) & if ~ x le 0.5, \\ (0.5,0.2,1) & otherwise, \] with gamma = 2. CrefoscillationFig presents the numerical solutions at t = 0.4 obtained using BP-OEDG, BPDG, and conventional DG schemes. One can see that the BPDG and conventional DG schemes introduce spurious numerical oscillations, while the results of BP-OEDG scheme are free of oscillations. nodes.statement: In this example, we compare the BP-OEDG scheme with global (Crefsec:global) and local invariant domains (Crefsec:local). Consider the following initial condition: \[ (rho,v,c)(x,0) = (1times 10^-12,10,1) & if ~ x < 0.25, \\ (0.8,0.5,1) & if ~ 0.25 le x < 0.985, \\ (0.5,400,1) & if ~ x ge 0.985. \] The parameter gamma = 0. The numerical results obtained by the locally and globally BP-OEDG schemes are shown in Creffig:LG. As one can see, even with a global constraint w le w_max enforced, a non-physical velocity overshoot can still be observed in the numerical results obtained by the globally BP-OEDG scheme. This is due to the global w upper bound (approx 399.37) being much larger than the local w upper bound (approx 0.30) near x = 0.25. In this case, enforcing a global constraint w le w_max can no longer help mitigate the v-overshoot in the vicinity. nodes.statement: In this example, we compare the HB and GHMW junction conditions. We consider a diverging junction connected to one outgoing road (Road 1) and two incoming roads (Road 2--3). The initial conditions on these roads are given by (rho^(1),rho^(2),rho^(3))(x,0) = (2,4,6) and (y^(1),y^(2),y^(3))(x,0) = (12,24,72). With respect to the GHMW networking setting, the priority vector is boldsymbolbeta = (1/2,1/2)^top. For HB network setting, please note that the priority vector boldsymbolbeta is determined by the traffic demands on the incoming roads. The BP-OEDG scheme is adopted to solve these problems, and the obtained numerical results are presented in Creffig:T7. As one can see, the discontinuities on Roads 2 and 3 are all well resolved without oscillations, while the contact discontinuities on Road 1 are slightly smeared. In Creffig:T7b, the discontinuity in c is resolved without overshoots or undershoots, demonstrating that the proposed BP-OEDG method preserves the minimum and maximum principles of c. nodes.statement: In this example, we test the propose BP-OEDG scheme on a traffic simulation over a network involving seven roads and three junctions, as depicted in Creffig:T8. The initial conditions are given by & rho^(1)(x,0) = rho^(2)(x,0) = rho^(6)(x,0) = 0.1, rho^(7)(x,0) = 10^-10, \\ & rho^(3)(x,0) = rho^(5)(x,0) = 0.18 + 10^-10 & if \; x in [0, 0.1], \\ 0.1 left[ 0.9 + (1-x) cosleft(frac25 pi (x - 0.1)0.9right)right] + 10^-10 & otherwise, \\ & rho^(4)(x,0) = 0.1 big[1 + x cos(25 pi x) big] + 10^-10, w_0^(r)(x) = 0.5, \; r = 1, cdots, 7. The parameter gamma = 2. At Junction A, the traffic distribution matrix is given by \( A = 0.5 & 0.5 \\ 0.5 & 0.5 \), and both Junctions A and B have the priority vector boldsymbolbeta = (0.5,0.5)^top. At Junction C, incoming traffic flux is evenly distributed between outgoing Roads 4 and 7. The proposed BP-OEDG scheme is used to conduct the simulation, and the results are presented in Creffig:T8. The trigonometric traffic waves initially located on Roads 3, 4, and 5, are accurately presented by the numerical results on a relatively coarse mesh. The discontinuity initially located on Road 4 passes through Junction A, and then introduces discontinuities on Roads 1 and 3, both of which are sharply resolved without oscillations. On Road 7, a discontinuity with near-vacuum state on its downstream side is captured without noticeable overshoots or undershoots. 	In this example, we test the propose BP-OEDG scheme on a traffic simulation over a network involving seven roads and three junctions, as depicted in \Cref{fig:T8}. The initial conditions are given by 
	\begin{align*}
		& 
		\rho^{(1)}(x,0) = \rho^{(2)}(x,0) = \rho^{(6)}(x,0) = 0.1, 
		\quad 
		\rho^{(7)}(x,0) = 10^{-10}, 
		\\
		& \rho^{(3)}(x,0) = \rho^{(5)}(x,0) =
		\begin{dcases}
			0.18 + 10^{-10} 
			& 
			{\rm if} \; x \in [0, 0.1],
			\\
			0.1 \left[ 0.9 + (1-x) \cos\left(\frac{25 \pi (x - 0.1)}{0.9}\right)\right] + 10^{-10} 
			& 
			{\rm otherwise},
		\end{dcases} \\
		& 
		\rho^{(4)}(x,0) = 0.1 \big[1 + x \cos{(25 \pi x}) \big] + 10^{-10},
		\quad
		w_0^{(r)}(x) = 0.5, \; r = 1, \cdots, 7.
	\end{align*}
	The parameter $\gamma = 2$. 
	At Junction A, the traffic distribution matrix is given by
	\(
	\mathcal{A} =
	\begin{pmatrix}
		0.5 & 0.5 \\
		0.5 & 0.5 
	\end{pmatrix}
	\),
	and both Junctions A and B have the priority vector $\boldsymbol{\beta} = (0.5,0.5)^\top$. 
	At Junction C, incoming traffic flux is evenly distributed between outgoing Roads 4 and 7. 
	The proposed BP-OEDG scheme is used to conduct the simulation, and the results are presented in \Cref{fig:T8}. 
	The trigonometric traffic waves initially located on Roads 3, 4, and 5, are accurately presented by the numerical results on a relatively coarse mesh. The discontinuity initially located on Road 4 passes through Junction A, and then introduces discontinuities on Roads 1 and 3, both of which are sharply resolved without oscillations.
	On Road 7, a discontinuity with near-vacuum state on its downstream side is captured without noticeable overshoots or undershoots.
	
	\begin{figure}[th!]
		\centering
		\includegraphics[trim=0 55 0 110,clip,width = 0.7\textwidth]{./Complex/46rho.pdf}
		\caption{\sf Example \ref{ex:T8}, BP-OEDG scheme, $\Delta x = 1/150$, $t = 0.25$. Reference solutions are depicted in black dashed lines.}
		\label{fig:T8}
	\end{figure}
